findings.why: This repeats the headline's 'removes dark spots' claim in the body; a face wash can't remove dark spots, and only a change in appearance can be claimed.
findings.fix: Visibly reduces the appearance of dark spots

findings.why: 'Spot-less' promises skin with no spots at all, an absolute result no cleanser can deliver; next to 'Fairness' in the product name it also reads as lightening (CLM-06).
findings.fix: Remove it; if a benefit line is needed, use 'For brighter-looking skin'.

findings.why: Germ claims position the face wash as antimicrobial, which is a drug/hygiene claim rather than cosmetic cleansing; it is acceptable only if legal clears it as purely mechanical cleansing.

rule_hit_review.why: 'Removes ... Dark Spots' is an elimination claim on a skin concern; removing dead skin cells is fine as a cleansing mechanism, but dark spots can only be claimed as 'visibly reduces the appearance of'.
'Fairness' in the product name makes lighter skin the goal, a direct breach of ASCI's skin-lightening guidelines; it has to go.
'Clinically proven face wash' doesn't say what was proven; it needs a product-specific study on file and its qualifier on the ad.

tone_read: This is fairness-category copy: a product name built on 'Fairness' and 'Spot Less', fragment bullets and removal promises, with no explanation of what the active does. It is the opposite of Minimalist's calm, educational, no-fear positioning.
language_read: The active is named loosely as 'Advanced Vitamin B3+' instead of Niacinamide, and with no concentration. Efficacy is unhedged elimination language ('removal', 'Removes', 'Spot-less') rather than 'visibly reduces the appearance of'.
